clinicalPearls: A rare inherited hyperfibrinolytic bleeding disorder caused by deficiency of alpha-2-antiplasmin, the principal physiological inhibitor of plasmin

Homozygotes bleed severely with a pattern resembling haemophilia, including delayed bleeding, haematomas, and umbilical stump or mucosal bleeding, while heterozygotes are usually mildly affected or asymptomatic
Bleeding is characteristically delayed and prolonged because clots form normally but are dissolved prematurely by unopposed plasmin
Routine coagulation screening tests (prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, platelet count, fibrinogen) are typically normal, which can obscure the diagnosis
A specific alpha-2-antiplasmin activity assay demonstrates the deficiency and is the key diagnostic test
Euglobulin clot lysis time is shortened, reflecting accelerated fibrinolysis
Antifibrinolytic therapy is the mainstay of treatment and prophylaxis around surgery and trauma
reference.pathophysiology: Alpha-2-antiplasmin, encoded by SERPINF2, is the main serpin that rapidly neutralises free plasmin and is cross-linked into the fibrin clot by factor XIII to protect it from lysis. In its deficiency, plasmin generated during fibrinolysis is inadequately restrained, so newly formed clots are degraded prematurely. Haemostatic plugs therefore form but fail to persist, producing a delayed bleeding phenotype despite normal clot formation and normal routine coagulation tests. The severity broadly parallels the residual inhibitor level, with homozygous patients most affected.
additionalDifferentials: Factor XIII deficiency (also causes delayed bleeding with normal screening tests)
Acquired hyperfibrinolysis (e.g. liver disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation)
additionalInvestigations: Alpha-2-antiplasmin activity assay to demonstrate the specific deficiency
Euglobulin clot lysis time to detect accelerated fibrinolysis
Standard coagulation screen (prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, fibrinogen), which is characteristically normal
Factor XIII assay to exclude a delayed-bleeding mimic
SERPINF2 gene analysis to confirm a congenital deficiency
Liver function tests to distinguish acquired hyperfibrinolysis
redFlags: Severe delayed bleeding after surgery, trauma, or dental extraction
Umbilical stump or mucosal bleeding in a homozygous neonate
Bleeding out of proportion to normal routine coagulation results
reference.prognosis: Homozygous patients can experience serious bleeding but generally respond well to antifibrinolytic therapy, allowing safe surgery and a good long-term outlook. Heterozygotes usually have a mild course. Prognosis depends on prompt recognition, as the normal screening tests can delay diagnosis.
pitfalls: Concluding there is no bleeding disorder because the routine coagulation screen is normal
Confusing it with factor XIII deficiency, which also causes delayed bleeding
Overlooking accelerated fibrinolysis by not requesting a clot lysis time
Failing to provide antifibrinolytic cover before invasive procedures
references: Hoffman: Hematology - Basic Principles and Practice
